task_row_model.query: Solve the nonhomogeneous ordinary differential equation y''' - 3y'' + 3y' - y = e^{x} x^2. Find the general solution, including a particular solution and justify the method (undetermined coefficients or the substitution y = e^x v(x)).

documents.content: As an elementary example of undetermined coefficients, consider y'' + y = sin x. The homogeneous equation has solutions cos x and sin x, so a trial particular solution for the right-hand side sin x would be of the form A cos x + B sin x. Substituting into the differential equation yields algebraic equations for A and B. If a resonance occurs (the trial lies in the homogeneous space), multiply by x until independence is restored. This standard procedure gives an explicit particular solution combined with the complementary solution to form the general solution.

Note that the operator L defined by L[y]=y''' - 3y'' + 3y' - y factors as (D-1)^3, since the characteristic polynomial is (r-1)^3. A useful reduction is to set y=e^x v(x); one finds (D-1)[e^x v]=e^x v', so iterating gives (D-1)^3[e^x v]=e^x v''' . Thus the nonhomogeneous equation reduces to v'''(x)=x^2. At this juncture one integrates v''' twice or three times to recover v up to polynomial constants; carrying out the integrations provides a polynomial of degree five plus integration constants, which then multiplies e^x to give a particular solution.

Legendre polynomials P_n(x) are solutions of the Legendre differential equation (1-x^2)y'' - 2x y' + n(n+1)y = 0. They form an orthogonal basis on [-1,1] with weight 1. The recurrence relation (n+1)P_{n+1}(x) = (2n+1)x P_n(x) - n P_{n-1}(x) generates higher-degree polynomials from lower-degree ones. Normalization typically sets P_n(1)=1. These properties underpin expansions of functions on [-1,1] and are widely used in solving boundary-value problems on spherical domains via series expansions.

The annihilator approach addresses resonance when the forcing is of the form e^{ax} times a polynomial. If the homogeneous operator has (r-a) as a root of multiplicity s, then the trial particular solution must be multiplied by x^s. For RHS e^{x} x^2, with root a=1 of multiplicity three, a suitable ansatz is y_p = e^{x} x^3 (A + B x + C x^2). Substituting this polynomial ansatz into the differential equation yields linear equations for A, B, C. This method systematically constructs a particular solution once the coefficient system is solved.

Observe L=y''' -3y'' +3y' - y factors as (D-1)^3. For y=e^x v(x) one has (D-1)[e^x v]=e^x v' and thus L[y]=(D-1)^3[e^x v]=e^x v'''. Setting L[y]=e^x x^2 gives v'''(x)=x^2. Integrate three times: v''=x^3/3 + C1, v'=x^4/12 + C1 x + C2, v=x^5/60 + C1 x^2/2 + C2 x + C3. Choosing C1=C2=C3=0 yields a particular v_p=x^5/60 and y_p=e^x x^5/60. The homogeneous solution is y_h=e^x(C0 + C1 x + C2 x^2). Hence the general solution is y=e^x(C0 + C1 x + C2 x^2 + x^5/60).
